text:
Recent work supports separating stable preferences from current intent while modeling elapsed time explicitly. [TLSTSRec (2024 online; 2025 issue)](https://doi.org/10.3233/IDA-240051) combines temporal representations with adaptive fusion of long- and short-term sequences. [Hierarchical long and short-term user preference modeling (2025)](https://journal.hep.com.cn/fcs/EN/10.1007/s11704-025-41181-y) uses dynamic routing to form multiple long-term preference vectors, self-attention for recent interactions, and similarity matching to retrieve the persistent interest most relevant to current activity. These approaches suggest that multiple persistent interests plus context-dependent selection may preserve useful older preferences without letting unrelated history dominate.

For a lightweight temporal baseline, [TALE (WSDM 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07382) learns linear item-to-item relationships using single-target augmentation, time-interval weighting, and trend-aware normalization. A practical synthesis—an architectural hypothesis, not an established result—is a SASRec recent-history encoder alongside a small bank of pooled long-term interest vectors, fused through a gate conditioned on observed historical gaps. Compare against simple recency pooling and TALE-style temporal weighting before adding complex latent dynamics. Purchase purpose, replacement need, and satisfaction remain unobserved hypotheses: timestamps establish elapsed time, not why an interest disappeared. Learn any decay or temporary suppression from next-item supervision and ablate it separately; use only timestamps available at prediction time, never the held-out target’s timestamp. None of these papers establishes gains on the pinned four-category RecHarness evaluation.
